title: Sing It, and Link Will Play It
summary: In the first game, Link plays songs on a small wind instrument called an ocarina to solve puzzles, travel fast, and call his horse, Epona. In the new Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you can hum or sing a song into the console's built-in microphone. If your tune matches a song Link can play, the game hears it and plays it for you. Players are already testing the system, and it works well. It can hear songs yelled into the microphone, played on a real instrument, or played from another screen. One player used a real ocarina to make Link play. Another got the game to hear a tune from an old video clip of a man singing something a bit like Epona's Song. The system is not perfect. If you sing something that does not sound like a song in the game, it will make its best guess. Players can usually use only five notes, but moving the analog stick lets them reach notes outside that range.
why_it_matters: If you like singing or playing music, you can now use your own voice or instrument to control a game character.

background_read: An ocarina is a small wind instrument that you play by blowing into it and covering holes to change the notes.
In the game, Link plays special songs on his ocarina to do helpful things, like solve puzzles, travel fast, and call his horse Epona.
The new version listens through the console's built-in microphone, so when a player hums or sings a song Link knows, the game can hear it and play it for them.
Article_Structure: WHO: Link, the hero of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and players testing the new remake.
WHAT: In the Switch 2 remake, players can hum or sing into the console's microphone, and the game hears the tune and plays the matching song for Link.
WHERE: In the new Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, using the console's built-in microphone.
WHY: So players can make Link play songs by singing, yelling, or using a real instrument, instead of only pressing buttons.
